hints: Focus on the ions present, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ can each form a precipitate if the other solution supplies a partner that makes an insoluble salt.
Recall that $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ provides $\text{OH}^-$ ions, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ provides $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ions, and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is the classic test for sulfate.
Check each mixture in turn for $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$, $\text{MgCO}_3$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$, then count how many actually give a white solid.
walkthrough:
**Identify what can precipitate**

Think of magnesium sulfate as $\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ plus $\text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq})$. A white precipitate forms only if we make an insoluble magnesium salt or an insoluble sulfate salt.

$$\text{MgSO}_4(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq})$$

**Test HCl and NH3**

With $\text{HCl}$, all chlorides formed are soluble, so $\text{MgCl}_2$ stays in solution and there is no precipitate. With $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$, ammonia acts as a base to give $\text{OH}^-$ which precipitates magnesium hydroxide.

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$$
$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{OH}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2(\text{s}) \text{ white}$$

**Test carbonate and barium nitrate**

Carbonate ions give sparingly soluble white magnesium carbonate. Barium ions give very insoluble white barium sulfate, this is the standard sulfate test.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{MgCO}_3(\text{s}) \text{ white}$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(\text{s}) \text{ white}$$

**Count them up**

No solid from $\text{HCl}$, but white solids from $\text{NH}_3$, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$. That is 3 precipitates in total.

options.A: 0 is wrong because three reagents do react. It assumes no insoluble Mg salt or Ba salt forms, forgetting the $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$, $\text{MgCO}_3$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$ precipitations.
options.B: 1 is wrong because it counts only one precipitate, often just $\text{BaSO}_4$. Students choosing this forget that $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ gives $\text{OH}^-$ for $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$ and that $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ gives $\text{MgCO}_3$.
options.C: 2 is wrong because it misses one of the three positives. A common error is to think $\text{MgCO}_3$ is soluble like Group 1 carbonates, or to think $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$ stays in solution.
options.D: 3 is correct. $\text{HCl}$ gives no precipitate, while $\text{NH}_3$ gives white $\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2$, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ gives white $\text{MgCO}_3$, and $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ gives white $\text{BaSO}_4$.
